title: How To Handle The Student Disrespect Sweeping The Country
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Responding to a post-pandemic spike in disrespect, Linsin argues that while the foundational SCM strategies — clear boundaries, consistency, calm enforcement — remain unchanged, teachers now need to elevate their nonverbal and interpersonal presence to match the moment. He details seven specific teacher behaviors: commanding body language and sharp dress, purposeful and sustained eye contact, a bold and unwavering speaking voice, blunt directness without hedging, longer strategic pauses to give words more weight, silent and unreactive handling of disrespectful outbursts, and brief after-the-fact 'debriefing' for students who genuinely don't realize their tone was disrespectful. He frames the underlying cause of rising disrespect as uncertain — pandemic isolation, screen addiction, or broader social anger — but insists teachers must adjust their presence regardless of cause, becoming a visibly stronger leader without becoming aggressive or vengeful. The recurring theme is that the teacher, not the student or the moment, must set the classroom's tone and culture.
points: The seven recommended teacher behaviors — body language, eye contact, voice, directness, pausing, silent enforcement, and brief debriefing — are offered as adaptations to rising post-pandemic disrespect.
Timid, hesitant body language and a mousy speaking voice now invite disrespect where they might once have been tolerated.
When a student is disrespectful, the recommended response is silence and calm enforcement rather than any visible reaction, since reacting rewards the behavior.
Some students genuinely don't recognize their tone as disrespectful, warranting a brief, non-confrontational after-the-fact explanation rather than a lecture.
The teacher, not the student or the broader social climate, is responsible for setting the classroom's tone and culture.
quotes: Since returning to in-person learning, respect has taken a nosedive.
You must take up space by standing tall with your shoulders back and head up. Walk and move with purpose or stand still and in one place .
You must speak boldly. Use your adult voice, even with younger students. Be clear and unwavering.
When you speak, let your instructions and directives hang heavy in the air. Wait them out. Let them settle. Say your peace and then zip it.
When you show that it doesn’t get under your skin, that you don’t take their disrespect personally, students stop doing it.
